3D-Printed Compressed-Air Engine

Designed and built a single-cylinder air engine through two printed prototypes, going from a binding first version to a smoother, bearing-supported one. A third revision is in progress.

Role
Designer & Maker
Timeline
Ongoing, personal project
Tools
CAD, FDM Printing
Status
V3 in progress
Outcome

A single-cylinder air engine built to practice crank kinematics and design for FDM, inspired by Tom Stanton. Two revisions printed and running on compressed air; V2 added a 0.127 mm diametral clearance allowance, metal hardware, and bearings, and turns noticeably smoother than V1. V3 is in progress to close out rod-boss rigidity and O-ring sealing.

My contribution
  • Designed the crank mechanism and packaging in CAD
  • Printed, assembled, and ran two full revisions
  • Diagnosed each failure mode and specified the fix for the next revision
  • Selected hardware and bearings to replace printed pins and shafts
Objective & Constraints
Kinematics
Single-cylinder crank mechanism that turns continuously on compressed air without binding through the stroke
Design for FDM
Fits specified with numeric allowances rather than nominal CAD dimensions, since printed features drift
Friction & wear
Rotating interfaces carried on bearings and metal hardware instead of printed pins and shafts
Sealing
Piston O-ring seals consistently across the stroke, still open, targeted in V3
Development

Each revision targets the failure mode the last one exposed.

V1: Concept
Failure: loose, out-of-round printed fits
Binds under load
V2: Fit & bearings
Fix: 0.127 mm diametral clearance allowance on press-fits, M2 bolts, bearings
Smoother, thin rod-boss deforms
V3: Sealing
Plan: thicker boss, datasheet O-ring groove
In progress
V1: Concept pass
Hand sketch (left), CAD (middle), 3D-printed components laid out (right)
  • Packaging and linkage geometry validated
  • Failed: press fits varied part to part, printed shafts out of round mechanism bound under load
  • Response: specify numeric allowances, move shafts and rods to metal hardware
V2: Fit, hardware & bearings
Hand sketch of redesign (left), CAD / assembly (middle), motion study (right)
  • 0.127 mm diametral clearance allowance on press fits
  • Printed pins and rods → M2 bolts in flush counterbores
  • Bearings added at the input and along the linkage
  • Result: motion noticeably smoother, assembly repeatable
Laid-out assembly of V2 (left), piston subassembly with new bearings (middle), full assembly (right)
  • Open: thin piston-rod wall deforms under press-in hardware → dislodges a bearing
  • Open: O-ring doesn't seal consistently with the current groove
V3: Refinement of clearances
Hand sketches, V3 concept
  • Thicker rod boss to survive the press fit
  • O-ring groove set from datasheet depth, width, and squeeze
  • Bearing retainer so it can't walk out under load
Engineering Decision

Printed press-in shafts caused friction and inconsistent fits, so V2 uses bolted metal hardware and bearings. That fixed the binding and left rod-boss thickness and O-ring sealing for V3.

Results (to date)
Two prototypes completed
Compressed air drives the mechanism; V2 runs smoother than V1 with fewer binding points
Improvements added
Tighter fits, metal hardware, and added bearings improved durability and made assembly repeatable
Open items
Rod-boss deformation under press-fit; inconsistent sealing at the O-ring groove
